comments.comment: 26:38  I don't think, "feminism" tells men, they are toxic. At least my brand of feminism acknowledges toxic masculinity as a structural problem. This is something that society has done to men, too, like you said it before about women. I mean - how does masculinity BECOME toxic? It happens when a future man is still a little boy and gets told "to man up" when he cries or to "learn to defend yourself" when be's being bullied. And when he's being bombarded with TV commercials aimed at boys, that show robots and space soldier toys with an ultramasculine, deep voice in the background praising them and explosions and whatnot, while the next spot, aimed at girls, shows you princesses in pink houses while high-pitched women's voices tell you about how you can make jewellery with your (girl) friends to adorn yourself and the princess.  IMHO, toxic masculinity can not be ended by men "just stopping". Of course, that needs to happen too - grown men should become aware of these things and try to consciously work against them, just as grown women need to consciously work against the toxic ideas they have been fed. But it is as important to change how we raise children! For example, I am active in a community garden and there are also some older women and they sometimes say things that sit wrong with me. There was a boy who wanted to use the pickaxe to dig a hole and one woman said, he has to wait until men are present, implying that we women would not be able to show him how to use it. So I was like: "Don't tell the boy that nonsense - he'll believe it in the end!", took the pickaxe and went with him to show him how to use it.  Or when a group of boys on the adjacent playground excluded a girl to come onto the multi-person swing with them, while shouting: "No girls on here!" I went there, told them that excluding girls is not good behaviour. They said, "But we're swinging very heavily and she'll not like it because she's a girl." I stopped the swing, let the girl climb on and when she was settled, I said: "See, she's as capable of doing that as you:"  And when a boy was being beaten by another one, I went and tried to comfort him. (It wasn't very successful, because I think he didn't trust me enough, but I tried.)  Anyway, I try to encourage boys to be kind, but also show them it's ok to be vulnerable and ask for help. (Same for girls, of course.)  Anyway; my understanding of feminism does include uplifting men. There is such a thing as the pro-feminist men's movement. They work alongside feminists and vice versa. IMHO, feminism is only called "feminism", because anything "feminine" or associate with "feminine" is being devalued in our society. Toxic masculinity is also rooted in this. If you're vulnerable, you run a risk to be labelled as "weak" => "gay" => "like a woman". And obviously, the worst thing a man can be in our society is "like a woman". That's also while some men feel the constant need to elevate themselves above women and demonstrate to other heterosexual males, how heterosexual male they are themselves. Women can only exist as prey in such a way of thinking, not as equal partners.  So, in my understanding the first goal of feminism is, to give back value to "the feminine" (meaning things that are traditionally being considered feminine). Once it's not shameful anymore to be nurturing, non-aggressive and accommodating others (to a certain degree), etc., the next goal would be to completely dissolve the categorization into "feminine" and "masculine" for character traits. This finds its practice in encouraging men to be less aggressive and more caring, and encouraging women to be more assertive and confident. Hopefully, at one point, the genders will find themselves on equal footing without being restricted by their traditional roles.
